- **Before meals**: antibiotics (general handout advice). **NSAIDs**: one hour before or two hours after meals.
- Antacids: separate from other drugs; not with milk; take with 8 oz of water; avoid within 30 minutes of sucralfate and one to two hours of other anti-ulcer drugs.
- Do not open or crush enteric-coated, sustained-release tablets or capsules.

## Priority nursing actions
Confirm the order, then the timing rule; if the order conflicts with a safe rule, clarify before giving.

## Client teaching
Take at the same time each day; do not stop suddenly.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which instruction is correct for a client starting sertraline?" -> morning. "A client takes a tricyclic: when?" -> bedtime.

## Related topics
[[Antidepressant Classes: TCA, SSRI and MAOI Drug Review]], [[Antacids]], [[Peptic Ulcer Drugs: PPIs, H2 Blockers and Sucralfate]], [[Diuretics: Thiazide, Loop, Osmotic and Potassium-Sparing]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout is not consistent (for example, beta-blockers on an empty stomach and calcium channel blockers with food); confirm per drug.

title: Drugs That Cause Sun Sensitivity or Need Sun Protection
body:
## What it is
Several drugs make skin burn more easily. The standard teaching is to avoid direct sunlight and cover up.

## Must-know facts (from the handout)
- Antipsychotics: avoid direct sunlight.
- Chlordiazepoxide (Librium): avoid excessive sunlight.
- Sulfonamides (including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole): photosensitivity; avoid direct sunlight.
- Tetracyclines: phototoxicity.
- Fluoroquinolones: photosensitivity.
- Griseofulvin: avoid sunlight.

## Priority nursing actions
- Teach protective clothing, hats and sunscreen; report rash or blistering.
- Skin reaction is not a medical emergency alone, but combined with fever, mouth sores or breathing trouble it is (sulfonamide and allergic reactions).

## How the exam asks about it
"Which instruction should be included for a client receiving a sulfonamide?" -> fluids and sun avoidance.

## Related topics
[[Tetracyclines, Fluoroquinolones and Aminoglycosides: Nursing Cautions]], [[Antipsychotic Drugs: Side Effects and Extrapyramidal Symptoms]], [[Sulfonamides and Urinary Anti-Infectives]], [[Antifungals]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout does not give a complete list; other drug classes also cause photosensitivity.

title: Drugs Unsafe in Narrow-Angle Glaucoma and Other Contraindication Groups
body:
## What it is
Contraindication lists in the handout repeat the same groups. Spotting the group is faster than memorising each drug.

## Must-know facts
- **Narrow-angle glaucoma**: anticholinergic drugs (including those for ulcers), antiemetics, antihistamines, ipratropium bromide, benzodiazepine anxiolytics.
- **Bronchial asthma / COPD**: non-selective beta-blockers (bronchospasm); NSAIDs in asthma; antihistamines in acute asthma.
- **Pregnancy**: barbiturates, lipid-lowering drugs, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors, lithium, oral hypoglycemic agents.
- **Intestinal obstruction**: cholinesterase inhibitors, antiemetics, laxatives, aluminum antacids (risk).
- **Ulcerative colitis**: antidiarrheals.
- **Increased ICP, CVA, severe hypertension**: general anesthetics; mucolytics with high ICP.
- **Heart block / ventricular arrhythmia**: digoxin.
- **Severe hypotension / hypovolemia**: nitrates.

## Priority nursing actions
Review the history for the disease group **before** the first dose; hold and clarify if a match.

## How the exam asks about it
Client with glaucoma, asthma or pregnancy is given an order; choose the drug or answer that is unsafe.

## Related topics
[[Antihistamines]], [[Antiemetic Drugs]], [[Alpha and Beta Adrenergic Blockers]], [[Drugs That Harm Organs, Stain Teeth or Cause Disulfiram Reactions]]

## Check against your textbook
This note regroups handout lines; verify groups for individual drugs.

title: Extrapyramidal Symptoms: Dystonia, Pseudoparkinsonism, Akathisia and Tardive Dyskinesia
body:
## What it is
EPS are movement side effects of antipsychotics that block dopamine. The handout names four.

## Must-know facts
- **Acute dystonia**: sudden, painful muscle spasm of neck, jaw, tongue or eyes; early onset.
- **Pseudoparkinsonism**: tremor, stiffness, shuffling, mask-like face, like Parkinson's disease.
- **Akathisia**: a feeling of inner restlessness; cannot sit still.
- **Tardive dyskinesia**: late-developing, repetitive abnormal movements (lip smacking, tongue movements); can be permanent.
- Anticholinergic antiparkinson drugs are used to ease some EPS (general knowledge, confirm in text).

## Assessment
Watch movements, posture, gait, speech and swallowing at each contact. Ask about restlessness.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Dystonia that affects the tongue or throat threatens the airway: assess airway first and call the provider.
2. Report any new EPS; do not wait for the next visit.
3. Do not stop the drug suddenly; the provider decides.
4. Safety: help with gait and falls.

## Client teaching
Report any unusual movements or stiffness; avoid alcohol and driving; keep up mouth care.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the description to the name; choose which EPS is the emergency.

## Related topics
[[Antipsychotic Drugs: Side Effects and Extrapyramidal Symptoms]], [[Antiparkinson Drugs: Levodopa, Carbidopa and Anticholinergics]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists the four names without descriptions; descriptions here are standard textbook content. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is not in the handout.

title: Inotropic, Chronotropic and Dromotropic Effects
body:
## What it is
Three terms describe how a drug changes the heart. They explain digoxin, dopamine and the pressors.

## Must-know facts
- **Inotrope**: changes force of contraction. Positive inotrope = stronger squeeze.
- **Chronotrope**: changes heart rate. Positive = faster, negative = slower.
- **Dromotrope**: changes conduction through the AV node. Positive = faster conduction.
- **Digoxin**: positive inotropic, negative chronotropic (stronger, slower).
- **Adrenergic agonists for shock**: positive inotrope and positive chronotrope; they raise cardiac output.
- **Dobutamine**: raises contractility without changing rate or oxygen demand much.
- **Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers**: lower rate and force, so less oxygen demand.

## Priority nursing actions
Check apical pulse and blood pressure before giving; report a slow heart rate (digoxin hold-point in handout: below 60 in adults, below 90 in infants).

## How the exam asks about it
"Which action describes digoxin?" -> stronger, slower beat.

## Related topics
[[Cardiac Glycosides: Digoxin]], [[Vasopressors for Hypotension and Shock]], [[Beta-Blockers for Angina and Dysrhythmias]]

## Check against your textbook
Dromotropic definition is minimal in the handout.
